appliesWhen: the agreement is silent on stamp duty, or states it is being executed on plain paper / unstamped
plainEnglish: An instrument that is not duly stamped cannot be admitted as evidence in court, or acted upon by a public officer, until the deficient duty (and usually a penalty) is paid. This does not make the tenancy itself illegal, but it can leave you unable to prove the agreed terms if a dispute reaches court.
negotiationAsk: Ask for the agreement to be executed on stamp paper of the correct value for your state, or e-stamped, before you sign.

appliesWhen: the lease term (including any renewal that takes it past one year, or where yearly rent is reserved) exceeds one year and the document is not registered
doesNotApplyWhen: the lease term is genuinely 11 months or less with no automatic renewal, which is why this duration is common practice
plainEnglish: A lease of immovable property for more than one year must be registered. An unregistered document that should have been registered cannot be used as evidence of the terms of the lease, and does not by itself create a valid leasehold interest. This is the legal reason so many Indian rental agreements are written for exactly 11 months.
negotiationAsk: If the term exceeds a year, ask for the document to be registered rather than relying on an unregistered long-term agreement.

appliesWhen: your state has adopted the Model Tenancy Act (or a state law with an equivalent cap) and the security deposit demanded exceeds 2 months' rent for a residential tenancy
doesNotApplyWhen: your state has not adopted the Model Tenancy Act, in which case no statutory cap applies and this is a matter of negotiation, not law
plainEnglish: The Model Tenancy Act caps residential security deposits at 2 months' rent (6 months for commercial), but it is a model law that only takes effect where a state has adopted it. Large deposits (8-10 months) are common practice and lawful in states that have not adopted the Act.
negotiationAsk: Ask which state law governs this tenancy and whether a deposit cap applies there; if it does, ask for the deposit to be reduced accordingly.

appliesWhen: assessing whether the agreement specifies a deposit refund timeline on vacating
plainEnglish: The Model Tenancy Act requires the deposit (less lawful deductions) to be returned to the tenant on the date of taking back vacant possession. Where the state has not adopted the Act, no fixed statutory timeline applies and the refund period is whatever the agreement specifies.
negotiationAsk: Ask for a specific refund date or window (e.g. within 15 days of handover) to be written into the agreement.

appliesWhen: assessing whether the agreement gives the landlord a right to enter without advance notice to the tenant
plainEnglish: Where the Model Tenancy Act applies, a landlord must give at least 24 hours' notice before entering the premises for inspection or repairs, except in a genuine emergency. Where it does not apply, this protection exists only if the agreement itself provides it.
negotiationAsk: Ask for a clause requiring at least 24 hours' written or message notice before any entry, except emergencies.

appliesWhen: the clause purports to let the landlord interrupt the tenant's possession, or enter and use the premises, at will during the tenancy
plainEnglish: The lessee's right to hold the property without interruption from the lessor, so long as rent is paid and covenants observed, is a default legal incident of every lease under the Transfer of Property Act. A clause trying to strip this away entirely conflicts with the basic legal nature of a tenancy.
negotiationAsk: Ask for the clause to be removed or reworded so the landlord's access is limited to reasonable, notified purposes.

appliesWhen: the clause absolutely bars the tenant from approaching a court, rent authority, or consumer forum to enforce their rights under the agreement
doesNotApplyWhen: the clause only fixes which court has territorial jurisdiction, without removing the right to approach a court at all
plainEnglish: A clause that completely removes your right to go to court or a statutory authority over this agreement is void. A clause that simply names which city's courts will hear a dispute is a different, and usually valid, thing.
negotiationAsk: Ask for the clause to be limited to fixing venue, not removing your right to sue.

section: Section 23 (unconscionability as a factor, not a standalone voiding rule)
appliesWhen: the tenant is locked in (liable for rent or forfeits deposit on early exit) for a period materially longer than any commitment the landlord makes not to terminate early
plainEnglish: Lock-in clauses that bind only the tenant, with no matching commitment from the landlord, are common and lawful, but one-sided. They are worth flagging and negotiating.
negotiationAsk: Ask for a matching notice obligation on the landlord, or a reduced lock-in period with a defined early-exit deposit forfeiture instead of full rent liability.

section: Section 73-74 (compensation must reflect actual loss, not an arbitrary forfeiture)
appliesWhen: the clause lets the landlord deduct 'any amount they deem fit' from the deposit for damage, without requiring an itemised list or estimate
plainEnglish: A landlord can only recover its actual, reasonable cost of repairing damage beyond normal wear and tear; a blanket right to withhold the deposit without justification is enforceable only to the extent of a genuine, provable loss.
negotiationAsk: Ask for a joint inspection and itemised deduction list to be a condition of any deposit withholding.

appliesWhen: the clause allows the landlord to revise rent during the fixed term at its own discretion, without a pre-agreed formula or notice period
doesNotApplyWhen: your state has adopted the Model Tenancy Act, under which mid-term revision must follow the agreement's own terms and cannot be unilateral
plainEnglish: Where the Model Tenancy Act does not apply, rent escalation is purely a matter of what the agreement says, and an open-ended 'landlord may revise rent at will' clause is lawful but heavily one-sided.
negotiationAsk: Ask for a fixed annual escalation percentage stated in the agreement, applicable only at renewal, not mid-term.

appliesWhen: the clause purports to let the landlord terminate the tenancy and require the tenant to vacate with no notice period, for a lease that does not itself fix a different notice requirement
plainEnglish: In the absence of a contract term to the contrary, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes requires six months' notice to terminate, and other leases require 15 days' notice, ending with the end of a tenancy month. Where a residential rent-control statute applies in your state, it may impose further protection against eviction without due process (e.g. a court or rent-authority order) even where the agreement purports to allow summary eviction.
negotiationAsk: Ask for a defined notice period before termination, and clarify whether a local rent control law adds further protection.

appliesWhen: the clause prohibits the tenant from subletting or transferring the tenancy without the landlord's written consent
plainEnglish: A landlord's right to prohibit subletting without consent is a standard, enforceable term and is in fact the default position under the Transfer of Property Act even if the agreement is silent.

appliesWhen: assessing who bears responsibility for repairs and normal upkeep during the tenancy
plainEnglish: In the absence of a contrary agreement, the tenant must keep the property in the condition it was received (fair wear and tear excepted) and hand it back in that condition; structural repairs are typically a landlord responsibility. The agreement can validly reallocate this, so long as it does so clearly.
negotiationAsk: Ask for the agreement to state explicitly who pays for structural repairs versus routine maintenance.

appliesWhen: the clause is silent on, or restricts, the tenant's right to remove fixtures they installed at their own cost
plainEnglish: A tenant has a default right to remove fixtures they attached to the property at their own expense, before handing back possession, provided the property is restored to its original condition. An agreement can lawfully restrict this if it says so clearly.
negotiationAsk: Ask for the agreement to confirm your right to remove fixtures you install, subject to restoring the property.

appliesWhen: assessing whether the landlord has a duty to disclose defects in the property not discoverable by ordinary inspection
plainEnglish: A landlord has a default duty to disclose material defects in the property that are not visible on a reasonable inspection and that the tenant is unaware of. A clause disclaiming 'as-is, all defects accepted' shifts risk to the tenant and can be flagged, though such clauses are common and generally enforceable for defects a reasonable inspection would reveal.
negotiationAsk: Ask for a walk-through inspection report to be attached as a schedule to the agreement, noting existing condition and defects.

appliesWhen: assessing what happens to the tenancy if the landlord sells or mortgages the property during the lease term
plainEnglish: If the landlord transfers the property, the new owner steps into the landlord's rights and obligations under the existing lease; a validly created tenancy is not automatically terminated by a sale, unless the lease itself is registered as being personal to the original landlord.
negotiationAsk: Ask for a clause confirming the tenancy survives a change of ownership on the same terms.

appliesWhen: the agreement demands rent for multiple months in advance, in addition to the security deposit, with no statutory cap in a state that has not adopted the Model Tenancy Act
plainEnglish: Advance rent on top of a security deposit is lawful where no state cap applies, but stacks up-front cost heavily against the tenant and is negotiable in practice even where not legally required.
negotiationAsk: Ask for advance rent to be reduced or waived given the security deposit already covers the landlord's risk.

appliesWhen: the clause on utility bills, maintenance charges, or society dues is vague about who pays what and by when
plainEnglish: Vague cost-sharing clauses are not void, but they are a common source of disputes precisely because they are unclear, and an unclear term is generally construed narrowly rather than in the drafter's favour.
negotiationAsk: Ask for exact charges (electricity, water, society maintenance, parking) and the paying party to be itemised.

appliesWhen: the clause makes renewal entirely at the landlord's discretion, with no right of first refusal for the tenant
plainEnglish: Landlord-discretion renewal clauses are standard and enforceable; Indian law does not give a residential tenant an automatic right to renew absent a specific rent-control statute that says otherwise.
negotiationAsk: Ask for a right of first refusal to renew on similar terms, notified a fixed number of days before expiry.

appliesWhen: assessing the notice period the tenant must give before vacating
plainEnglish: In the absence of a contrary agreement, 15 days' notice ending with the tenancy month is the statutory default for most residential leases. The agreement can validly extend this, and a longer notice period (30-60 days) is common and enforceable.
negotiationAsk: Confirm the exact notice period and that it is symmetric with what the landlord must give you.
